English: Crookhaven, April 7th, 1897.
I have heard tell of a woman saint that met the devil on a night, when the ground was covered with snow & he asked her some questions;

Manx: “C’red ta ny s’gilley na sniaghtey syn oie?”
English: What is whiter than snow in the night?

Manx: Dooyrt ee “Ny s’gilley na shen ta flaunys thie Yee”
English: [She said] Whiter than that is the effulgence of God’s house.
“What is worse than a woman?”

Manx: “Ta’n mioleyder broigh ny smessey na shen.”
English: “The dirty tempter is worse than that.”
I have forgotten the rest of the dialogue.

Manx: Ben vooar ruy v’ec Sandy Ling
English: Sandy Ling had a big brown wife,

Manx: Ceau braagyn yiarn as oasheryn tin.
English: wearing iron shoes & tin stockings.
I know very little about farming for I never had any delight in it; the sea for me when I was a young man. But the old farmers called the
plough
(& the) harrows
(and) ploughing
(and) harrowing
(and) butts[1] of potatoes, (like they make in Ireland,)
(and) corn butts

— The farmers make no such butts in the Island since they ... ... have got reaping machines, but before that every reaper had his own length to cut. I remember two men plowing – one leading the horses the other holding the plow.

rowing oars
mizen.
Jib

Cuirr yn leein
Coyrt er boayrd

I have heard tell of a ghost that was coming home, so his friends got a blacksmith to make an iron cross to lay on the grave. It appears the ghost was not in the grave when the cross was laid on it, but he came before they left the grave, and said —
(lift this)
and then disappeared. And the people said the blacksmith never did any good afterward.

I was talking to a Catholic priest last summer. He could read my Manx writing well enough, & he repeated some Manx songs that he had learned from Tom Kermode in Bradda. He said that he had them published six years ago. But Tom Kermode, the blind man, is dead & buried now & all his songs are sung.

I remember the night when the Royal Charter was lost[2]. I was in a fishing boat in Howth harbour, about nine miles from Dublin; and as it was very stormy & rough in the harbour we were on deck all night. And about ten o’clock at night – a big stack of fire went over the harbour at a great height. It made a great illumination. No one could tell what it was, but some were of the opinion that it was a sign of the loss of the herring fleet, but the boats got home safe enough. I have never seen such a thing since – whatever it was or whatever it meant. I fancy many of the old weather sayings never come to pass now for they saw the Island is gone further North than it used to be and that will make a great difference in the weather, so the old folklore must be wrong about the weather.
Notes: [2]  The Royal Charter] a steam clipper that was lost off the cost of Anglesey as a consequence of The Royal Charter Storm on the 26th of October 1859, with the loss of an estimated 450 lives.

English: From Faragher of Cregneish

Manx: Oie innyd bee dty vinnyd[3] lane,
English: Ash Wednesday Eve your runnet[4] will be full.
Notes:
[3]  dty vinnyd] — dty vinnid — ‘your rennet’. 
[4]  Runnet] likely ‘rennet’ taken to mean ‘stomach’.

Manx: Shimmey y gaue ta shin currit lesh ny hrooid.
English: Many’dangers we have been brought through.

Manx: Yn magher caggee, yn boayl dy phrowal foays yn chliwe
English: The battlefield is the place to prove the goodness of the sword.

Manx: Te ny s’aashagh dy gheddyn ayns boirey na dy gheddyn ass.
English: It is easier to get in bother than to get out.

Manx: Cha jean yn mainshter cur shin ass yn school cre erbee cha staghylagh as ta shin.
English: The master will not put us out of the school however stupid we are.

Manx: Ollick gennal as blein feer vie
English: A Merry Xmas an’ very good year,

Manx: Luck as slaynt da’n slane lughtthie
English: Luck & health to all the family,

Manx: Bea as gennalys riu bio ry cheilley
English: Life & health to you alive together;

Manx: Shee as graih eddyr mraane as deiney
English: Peace and love between men & women.

Manx: Ta imbagh cour dy chooilley nhee.
English: For every thing there is a season.

Manx: Cha vel scansh y voddee ort
English: [You are] As careless as the dogs.

Manx: Tra ta’n gheay coayl e[5] bree,
English: [When the wind loses its energy,
Notes: [5] e] ‘his’. [y] in the original. Ned beg Hom Ruy frequently uses ‘y’ for ‘e’ — ‘his’ / ‘her’.

English: Everything is at peace.]

Manx: Ta mee er chlashtyn ny shenn gheinney dy mennick gra; Lurg Laa Maayll mooar, dy row ‘daa faarkey goaill ayns unnane’.
English: I have heard the old men say often that ‘Two waves are going in one’ after St. Michael’s Day.

After St Michael’s day the wintry storms are coming on & the sea gets no rest & the waves are often rising higher than in the summer, so the old folks said that two waves were going in one for the sea was so much heavier.

I have heard it said that a woman with red hair was very unluckly to meet the first thing in the morning if going on a journey or on business,  but I think it all nonsense, what can that have to do with it, unless she is a witch – there is one not very far off & they say she is a witch. The old folks had this proverb about the time to go to bed & the time to get up;

Manx: Tra lhieys yn ghrian as tra irrys yn eean
English: When the sun sets, (to bed;)  when the birds rises (the time to get up.)
This was supposed to be after Old Patrick’s Day, which is the twenty-eighth of March.

Black cats — A black cat was reckoned very lucky in a house – one without a spot of any other colour, especially in a fisherman’s house. They believed that none of the men would be drowned while the black cat was alive. If a black cat came in the house while the women were churning & commenced to lick up the drops of milk sprinkled[6]
Notes: [6] Unfortunately, the significance of the cat licking the milk is not explained.

English: Cats often disappear when one of the family dies and are never seen again. I have heard this many times. My father and his cat were not very good friends, for he was teasing her too much; but after he died the cat disappeared & we never seen her since – nor heard any account of her.

Bees. The old fishermen thought it very lucky to catch the first bee they seen in April. It was the sign of a good herring season, they said. I have seen men chasing the first bee they saw for a long way & if they caught him they kept him in the purse; But if they did not catch him – it was a sign that his earnings would be light. When I saw one this morning it reminded me of the old practice of catching the first bee – but I think there is no one trying to catch the first bee as the present time.

There was a woman telling the other day about the mere maids [mermaids], and she said it was true enough, for those folks used to be very plentiful about the Island. She said when the old fishermen were out in the evenings setting their lines they used to have a long stone for an anchor, & when the lines were set they anchored with the stone and lay until the morning if the weather was favourable. They had an old pot in the boats for a fire place – I have seen some of the them myself in the highlands of Scotland. When lying at anchor in the evening they used to make porridge for supper, When the young mere-maids [mermaids] were smelling the porridge they would gather about the boat – but their fathers and mothers would not make so free as the young ones. She said they would come to the boat to get at the porridge and would help themselves with both their hands & eat as fast as they could swallow if the fishermen did not drive them away. She said it was the truth for she had heard the old folk telling it.

I suppose it has come down from father to son like other yarns, but it must have been long ago when the fairies are not so shy as they are at present. I suppose the mere-maids [mermaids] and their families are gone to Fairyland with the fairies, for meremaids & fairies have disappeared.

I cannot recollect anything more at present, So I must conclude, wishing you health & happiness, which is a rare thing in this world, for none are truly happy, for this world is not a permanent home though it is said that some have their portion here. But I would rather not enjoy the present but patiently await the happiness of the world to come.
Edward Faragher of Cregneish
April 1897
